title: Airbus CSO: Reflections on Farnborough and aviation sustainability
description:
Julie Kitcher is Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications at Airbus and a member of the company’s Executive Committee.
She oversees Airbus’ sustainability roadmap and communications strategy, and also chairs the Airbus Foundation.
Across the week, I saw this playing out in discussions ranging from climate adaptation and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) to the role of energy efficiency across the aviation sector.
SAF is now an established part of the aviation sustainability conversation.
What Farnborough revealed about the road ahead More than anything, Farnborough reinforced how interconnected the industry’s biggest challenges have become.
text:
Julie Kitcher is Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications at Airbus and a member of the company’s Executive Committee. She oversees Airbus’ sustainability roadmap and communications strategy, and also chairs the Airbus Foundation.

I felt a distinct shift at this year’s Farnborough International Airshow. Against a backdrop of high global fuel prices and geopolitical instability, conversations that once centred predominantly on decarbonisation and net zero are increasingly being framed through the lens of pragmatism, resilience and competitiveness.

In the industry, we call this the ‘Energy Trilemma’, which is the challenge of balancing emissions reduction with energy security and affordability.

Across the week, I saw this playing out in discussions ranging from climate adaptation and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) to the role of energy efficiency across the aviation sector. What struck me was not a retreat from sustainability ambitions, but a growing recognition that achieving them requires solutions that work in a complex global reality.

In many ways, Farnborough reflected an industry entering a new phase. One that’s focused less on ambitions and more on creating the conditions to deliver them.

Here are some of my key takeaways:

As climate change confronts Europe, adaptation is moving up the agenda

For much of my time as CSO, conversations at major industry events have centred on climate mitigation and the actions we’re taking to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

At this year’s Farnborough, however, adaptation featured much more prominently. Specifically, how our industry, and society more broadly, can strengthen resilience to the effects of climate change.

To me, this reflects an important evolution in the industry’s thinking. Climate change is no longer being discussed solely as an environmental challenge, but a resilience challenge that has direct implications for infrastructure, operations, and competitiveness.

That shift is unsurprising given the extreme weather Europe is experiencing, including record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires. President Emmanuel Macron’s description of the fires in France as the country’s biggest challenge since the Second World War underlined the scale of the threat.

As extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, I expect adaptation to become an increasingly important part of the sustainability conversation. The aerospace sector will be judged not only on its contribution to reducing emissions, but also on its ability to help societies anticipate, respond to, and recover from climate-related disruption.

Wildfires are one example. Aerospace technologies already play a critical role across the response ecosystem, from satellites that can detect hotspots and monitor the spread of fires, to aircraft and helicopters that support firefighting and emergency services on the ground.

SAF is shifting from promise to progress

While adaptation featured more prominently than in previous years, the energy transition remained firmly on the agenda.

SAF is now an established part of the aviation sustainability conversation. What was encouraging at Farnborough was the shift from discussing its potential to confronting the practical challenge of scaling production and accelerating adoption.

Investment will be central to making that happen. Across discussions with aviation leaders, airport operators and SAF producers, there was a clear recognition that scaling SAF will require significant financial commitment, disciplined capital allocation and long-term policy certainty.

It will also require deeper collaboration across the value chain. Our partnership with Air Canada to help strengthen the Canadian SAF ecosystem, announced at Farnborough, is one example of what this can look like in practice. Progress ultimately depends on building tangible, local ecosystems in which OEMs, airlines, fuel suppliers and airports work together.

Despite a challenging macro-economic environment, I came away encouraged by the level of collaboration on display. There was a clear collective focus on moving from ambition to implementation and that gives me reason for optimism.

The industry’s most immediate opportunity is often overlooked

There was one opportunity I felt deserved more attention.

While much of the industry’s focus is rightly on future fuels and technologies, there is also a significant opportunity to improve the energy efficiency of aviation today. Replacing older aircraft with the latest-generation models can reduce fuel consumption by 20-25%, lowering emissions while helping airlines manage costs in an increasingly challenging operating environment.

Aviation’s transition will unfold over decades, but that makes near-term action more important, not less. As we develop the next generation of aircraft and scale lower-carbon fuels, we should also make full use of the solutions already available to reduce emissions today.

As climate targets draw closer, I expect energy efficiency will move higher up the agenda as organisations look for practical ways to deliver measurable reductions.

What Farnborough revealed about the road ahead

More than anything, Farnborough reinforced how interconnected the industry’s biggest challenges have become. Decarbonisation, climate resilience and energy security can no longer be addressed in isolation.

Making progress will require a sustainability transition that works across all these dimensions. Reducing emissions while ensuring that aviation’s infrastructure, operations and supply chains remain resilient and competitive.

I left Farnborough feeling optimistic. Not because the challenges have become smaller, but because there is growing alignment across the industry on what practical progress requires.

The task is now to turn that alignment into action.

title: Steam-Powered Airline Concept Captures Aviation's Imagination
description:
A playful but persistent rumor about a “steam-powered airline” taking to the skies has been circulating online, blending historical anecdotes, speculative engineering and a dash of satire into one of aviation’s more unusual talking points this summer.
The “steam-powered airline” functions less as a literal project and more as a symbol of how far people are willing to stretch their imaginations when thinking about cleaner flight.
Sustainable aviation fuel, synthesized from waste, biomass or renewable electricity, is also gaining ground as a near-term option.
How Travelers Are Responding To The Steam Meme The spread of the steam-powered airline idea has prompted a mix of amusement and curiosity among travelers.
What It Signals For Aviation’s Next Chapter The rise of a fictional steam-powered airline may not alter aircraft design blueprints, but it does offer clues about public sentiment.
text:
A playful but persistent rumor about a “steam-powered airline” taking to the skies has been circulating online, blending historical anecdotes, speculative engineering and a dash of satire into one of aviation’s more unusual talking points this summer.

From Victorian Dreams To Viral Headlines

Publicly available information indicates that no modern commercial airline is preparing to operate steam-powered passenger services. Instead, the phrase has emerged as a shorthand for a wave of social media posts and forum discussions that imagine a retro-futurist carrier fueled by steam, often accompanied by whimsical artwork and tongue-in-cheek commentary about “bringing the age of steam back to aviation.”

The idea is not entirely detached from history. Early aviation pioneers did experiment with steam propulsion in light aircraft, drawing on technologies already well established in locomotives and ships. Those efforts, however, were quickly overtaken by the practical advantages of internal combustion engines, which offered far better power-to-weight ratios and were easier to integrate into small airframes.

What has changed today is the context. With decarbonization now a central challenge for aviation, the notion of steam has resurfaced in online conversations as travelers look for alternatives to fossil fuels and share eye-catching concepts. The “steam-powered airline” functions less as a literal project and more as a symbol of how far people are willing to stretch their imaginations when thinking about cleaner flight.

Reports from enthusiast communities suggest that the meme gained traction alongside broader interest in unconventional propulsion, from hydrogen-electric powertrains to hybrid-electric regional aircraft. References to steampunk aesthetics and classic rail travel have helped the idea resonate with audiences who see aviation as part of a wider cultural story about technology and nostalgia.

Why Steam And Scheduled Flights Do Not Mix

A key reason steam power never progressed into mainstream airline use lies in basic physics. Steam systems rely on boilers, condensers and large quantities of water, all of which add substantial weight. In commercial aviation, where every kilogram counts against payload and range, this makes steam a poor match for efficient operations.

Thermal efficiency is another obstacle. Modern gas turbines and advanced piston engines convert fuel to thrust far more effectively than traditional steam cycles sized for aircraft. That efficiency gap would force any hypothetical steam airliner to burn more energy to carry fewer passengers over shorter distances, undermining both economics and sustainability goals.

Safety and certification considerations also pose serious challenges. High-pressure steam systems demand extensive containment and redundancy. Integrating such hardware into a pressurized fuselage while meeting contemporary airworthiness standards would require radical design compromises. Public documentation on current aircraft programs shows manufacturers instead concentrating on propulsion architectures that build on existing certification pathways, such as turbofans compatible with sustainable aviation fuel or hybrid-electric systems.

In day-to-day airline operations, reliability is paramount. Complex steam equipment would increase maintenance burdens and ground time. Modern carriers, already working to optimize utilization and reduce delays, have little room for experimental configurations that significantly complicate ground handling and engineering support.

Real-World Alternatives Pushing Cleaner Flight

While a steam-powered airline remains firmly in the realm of speculative fiction, several concrete propulsion technologies are advancing that could reshape short-haul travel. Publicly reported test programs highlight progress in battery-electric aircraft designed for regional routes and training missions, as well as hybrid-electric concepts that combine conventional engines with electric motors for improved efficiency.

Hydrogen-electric powertrains, which use fuel cells to drive electric propellers, are another focus of industry investment. Test-bed aircraft have already flown with hydrogen-based systems supplying part or all of the propulsion on experimental flights, according to published coverage from manufacturers and aviation outlets. These efforts aim to cut inflight carbon dioxide emissions while fitting within recognizable aircraft configurations and airport operations.

Sustainable aviation fuel, synthesized from waste, biomass or renewable electricity, is also gaining ground as a near-term option. Airlines and aerospace companies have reported successful demonstrations of flights using high blends, and in some cases 100 percent, synthetic or bio-derived jet fuel in existing engines. Because SAF is compatible with today’s fleets and fueling infrastructure, it is widely seen as a bridge solution while more radical propulsion concepts mature.

Together, these avenues represent a pragmatic response to climate pressures. None involve a return to steam, but all tap into the same desire that fuels the steam-airline meme: a search for ways to keep people flying while dramatically cutting the environmental cost of air travel.

How Travelers Are Responding To The Steam Meme

The spread of the steam-powered airline idea has prompted a mix of amusement and curiosity among travelers. Social media threads and online travel communities show users trading mock boarding passes, imagined safety cards and tongue-in-cheek route maps for a fictional carrier that would pair brass fittings with panoramic observation lounges.

Alongside the humor, the concept has acted as a gateway for more serious questions. Some posters ask how steam engines actually work, while others compare them with jet turbines, hydrogen fuel cells or batteries. Educators and aviation enthusiasts have used the moment to share explanations of thrust, energy density and why certain technologies succeed in flight while others remain on the drawing board.

For travel brands and tourism organizations, the conversation underscores how narratives about technology shape perception. Even a fanciful idea like a steam-powered airline can influence how people think about the future of flight, especially when it is wrapped in compelling visuals and shared in viral formats. The attention suggests an appetite for clearer, more engaging communication about what sustainable aviation might realistically look like over the next two decades.

Some commentators also see the meme as a reaction to the sometimes abstract language of climate roadmaps and regulatory targets. By contrast, the image of a gleaming steamliner at a modern airport is instantly understandable, even if it is technically implausible. It offers a way to talk about change that feels tangible, story-driven and rooted in a familiar travel experience.

What It Signals For Aviation’s Next Chapter

The rise of a fictional steam-powered airline may not alter aircraft design blueprints, but it does offer clues about public sentiment. Travelers appear increasingly interested in how their journeys are powered and more willing to engage with complex engineering ideas when those ideas are presented in vivid, imaginative ways.

Aviation’s real transition will likely be led by less romantic, more incremental steps: higher-efficiency engines, cleaner fuels, lighter materials and smarter flight operations. Yet the enthusiasm surrounding speculative concepts suggests that there is room for creativity in how airlines and manufacturers talk about these advancements.

For now, the only steam most passengers will encounter is curling off a coffee cup in the departure lounge. Still, the notion of a steam-powered airline taking flight has earned its place in the wider conversation about where aviation has come from and where it might go next, acting as a reminder that even the most improbable ideas can inspire fresh thinking about the future of travel.

text:
SkyDrive rafforza la propria strategia di sviluppo internazionale affidandosi all’esperienza di Stéphane Ginoux, ex Presidente di Airbus Japan ed ex Responsabile delle attività Airbus nel Nord Asia, nominato Advisor della società con decorrenza dal 1° agosto 2026.

L’ingresso di Ginoux punta a sostenere il percorso di SkyDrive verso il lancio e la diffusione internazionale degli eVTOL, i velivoli elettrici a decollo e atterraggio verticale sui quali l’azienda giapponese sta costruendo la propria visione della mobilità urbana del futuro.

Con circa 30 anni di esperienza nell’industria aeronautica, Ginoux porta nella società competenze nello sviluppo del business, nelle partnership pubblico-private e industriali e nelle relazioni con aziende, governi e istituzioni di ricerca.

Un ruolo strategico per lo sviluppo in Giappone e Asia

Nel nuovo incarico di Advisor, Stéphane Ginoux fornirà supporto strategico a SkyDrive in diverse aree. Il suo contributo riguarderà in particolare lo sviluppo del business in Giappone e Asia, il coinvolgimento di governi, autorità locali e associazioni industriali e la collaborazione con i partner commerciali.

La società intende valorizzare anche l’ampia rete di relazioni costruita da Ginoux nel corso della sua carriera con interlocutori istituzionali e aziendali.

Per SkyDrive, infatti, lo sviluppo di un mercato sostenibile per gli eVTOL non dipende esclusivamente dalla realizzazione del velivolo. La futura diffusione di questa tecnologia richiede anche collaborazione in ambiti come operazioni, conformità normativa e sviluppo delle infrastrutture.

Il nuovo Advisor sarà quindi chiamato a mettere la propria esperienza internazionale al servizio di un progetto che punta prima all’introduzione degli eVTOL sviluppati in Giappone e successivamente alla loro espansione su scala globale.

Quasi 30 anni di esperienza nel settore aeronautico

Il percorso professionale di Stéphane Ginoux è strettamente legato all’industria aeronautica e alle relazioni tra Europa e Asia. Originario della Francia, arrivò in Giappone nel 1992 nell’ambito di un incarico del governo francese.

Ha lavorato presso il Ministero del Commercio Internazionale e dell’Industria del Giappone, oggi Ministero dell’Economia, del Commercio e dell’Industria, e presso la Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO). Successivamente ha operato nella sezione commerciale dell’Ambasciata di Francia in Giappone.

Nel 1996 è entrato in Eurocopter, oggi Airbus Helicopters, dando inizio a un lungo percorso all’interno del gruppo aeronautico.

Dalla fondazione di Airbus Helicopters Japan alla guida del Nord Asia

Nel 2009 Ginoux ha fondato Airbus Helicopters Japan. L’anno successivo è stato nominato Representative Director e Presidente di Airbus Japan, continuando contemporaneamente a guidare Airbus Helicopters Japan.

Dal 2016 ha ricoperto anche la posizione di Rappresentante di Airbus Group Japan, per poi diventare Responsabile del Nord Asia di Airbus, con responsabilità sulle attività del gruppo nella regione, inclusi Giappone e Corea del Sud.

Durante la sua permanenza in Airbus ha contribuito all’espansione del business degli aerei commerciali in Giappone, alla costruzione delle basi dell’attività nel settore degli elicotteri e al rafforzamento della collaborazione con aziende e istituzioni governative giapponesi.

Il suo percorso comprende inoltre iniziative dedicate all’aviazione sostenibile, tra cui attività relative al Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) e all’aviazione alimentata a idrogeno.

Dopo aver lasciato Airbus nel giugno 2025, Ginoux ha continuato a fornire consulenza strategica ad aziende giapponesi e internazionali.

SkyDrive verso il lancio commerciale di SKYDRIVE

Fondata ufficialmente nel 2018 dopo l’avvio dei test sui prototipi eVTOL nel 2014, SkyDrive sviluppa velivoli elettrici compatti a decollo e atterraggio verticale con l’obiettivo di rendere questa nuova forma di trasporto una componente della vita urbana.

Nel 2019 la società è diventata la prima azienda a effettuare in Giappone il volo di un eVTOL con equipaggio. Nel 2025 ha inoltre presentato il proprio primo prodotto, SKYDRIVE, attraverso voli dimostrativi all’Expo di Osaka, osservati da migliaia di visitatori nell’arco di un mese.

La produzione di SKYDRIVE è iniziata nel marzo 2024 presso uno stabilimento di Suzuki Motor Corporation, partner ufficiale di SkyDrive per la produzione.

Parallelamente, l’azienda sta lavorando con le autorità dell’aviazione civile del Giappone e degli Stati Uniti per ottenere la certificazione del velivolo, con l’obiettivo di avviarne il servizio nel 2028.

L’esperienza di Ginoux per la crescita internazionale

L’arrivo di Stéphane Ginoux assume particolare rilevanza nella fase in cui SkyDrive deve trasformare lo sviluppo tecnologico degli eVTOL in un’attività operativa capace di espandersi oltre il mercato domestico.

Le competenze maturate dal nuovo Advisor nella costruzione di partnership industriali e pubblico-private, unite alla conoscenza dei mercati aeronautici giapponese e asiatico, potranno sostenere il dialogo con gli attori necessari allo sviluppo dell’ecosistema eVTOL.

text:
Noida: India’s airport network is entering a new phase as Noida International Airport in Jewar and Navi Mumbai International Airport expand the capacity of two of the country’s most congested metropolitan regions. The shift is not only about accommodating more flights. It could reshape where jobs, logistics, housing and commercial activity grow around Delhi-NCR and Mumbai.

The two airports are being developed as additional capacity for regions where existing facilities face physical and operational constraints. Noida International Airport began passenger operations in June 2026 with an initial capacity of 12 million passengers a year. Its planned capacity is 70 million. Navi Mumbai International Airport has an initial capacity of 20 million passengers and is designed to scale to 90 million. For citizens, the bigger change will depend on connectivity beyond the airport gates. Noida’s project is planned as a multimodal hub linking road, rail and metro networks, while its cargo facilities are intended to strengthen connections with manufacturing and logistics clusters across western Uttar Pradesh. The airport’s cargo hub is designed for more than 250,000 tonnes annually in its initial configuration, with substantial scope for expansion.

Navi Mumbai faces a different urban challenge. Its value will depend heavily on how efficiently it connects with Mumbai and surrounding districts. The 21.8-km Atal Setu provides a major road link between the island city and Navi Mumbai, while further public transport connections are being planned. The real estate impact is already becoming visible around Jewar. Rising interest in residential land and development schemes shows how quickly airport infrastructure can alter land values and development expectations. That growth also creates a regulatory responsibility. Buyers assessing projects near the airport should verify approvals, land use, title and applicable RERA registration rather than treating proximity to an airport as a guarantee of returns. Recent YEIDA housing plans indicate that residential demand around Jewar is continuing to build.

Environmental performance will be another test. Noida has been positioned around resource-efficient infrastructure, while Navi Mumbai has outlined measures including solar generation, electric buses, water management and sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure. Yet the wider footprint matters as much as terminal efficiency: roads, construction, groundwater, waste and new housing can determine whether airport-led growth remains climate-resilient. The emergence of Noida International Airport and Navi Mumbai therefore marks more than an aviation capacity increase. Their success will ultimately be measured by whether faster travel is matched by reliable public transport, well-planned housing, responsible land development and employment opportunities for surrounding communities.

text:
The Indian sugar industry is undergoing a structural change as mills move away from a single-product model toward integrated biorefineries. This transition aims to insulate companies from the boom-and-bust cycles traditionally associated with sugar production. By diversifying into ethanol, compressed biogas (CBG), and advanced bio-chemicals like polylactic acid (PLA), mills are attempting to unlock multiple revenue streams from the same agricultural raw materials.

Diversification as a Survival Strategy

The push for biorefineries is driven by the government's ethanol blending program. By processing molasses, grain, and other feedstocks into ethanol, mills can maintain asset utilization even when sugar prices are low. Large players like Balrampur Chini Mills and E.I.D. Parry are already investing in advanced technologies, including the production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and bio-based plastics. This integration turns waste products, such as bagasse and press mud, into energy or fuel, creating a more circular and resilient business model.

The Immediate Margin Challenge

Despite the long-term strategic benefits, the financial reality for the current fiscal year is complex. Sugar companies are facing significant margin pressure due to a combination of rising input costs and stagnant ethanol procurement prices. While the government has encouraged the shift to ethanol, the procurement prices paid to mills have not kept pace with the rising cost of sugarcane cultivation.

For investors, this creates a situation where revenue growth from ethanol might not translate directly into higher bottom-line profitability if the cost-to-revenue ratio remains unbalanced. Profitability in the coming quarters will heavily depend on whether the government adjusts ethanol pricing to reflect the increased costs of production and raw materials.

Policy and Operational Risks

Investors must also track the government's regulatory stance on sugar availability. Because sugar is a sensitive commodity, the government often prioritizes domestic supply and price stability, especially ahead of festive seasons. This has led to periodic restrictions on the diversion of sugarcane juice or syrup toward ethanol production. When the government restricts ethanol output to protect domestic sugar supply, it directly impacts the revenue diversification plans of these mills.

Furthermore, there is an operational trade-off regarding the timing of the crushing season. Industry bodies have requested an early start to the 2026-27 crushing season to help ease market supply. While this may increase volume, it carries a risk of lower sucrose maturity in the cane, which leads to lower recovery rates—meaning mills produce less sugar per tonne of cane. This operational inefficiency can impact the profit margins of mills during the early months of the season.

What Investors Should Monitor

The transition to a biorefinery model is a multi-year process that requires substantial spending on infrastructure. Key monitorables for shareholders include the trend in ethanol procurement prices, updates on export or diversion policies, and the efficiency of new capacity utilization. Monitoring quarterly margins will be essential to determine if these companies can successfully balance their expanded operational footprints with the volatility of the underlying commodity markets.

text:
Aviation is often treated as one of oil's safest remaining markets. In 2026 that still looks like a reasonable assumption. Airlines are expected to consume around 104 billion gallons of fuel this year, sustainable aviation fuel remains below 1% of total use, and virtually every commercial passenger aircraft in service still depends on liquid hydrocarbons.

But that view risks making the same mistake the oil industry made with cars: looking at the installed fleet rather than at the technology competing for the next route.

On July 30, Archer's all-electric Midnight aircraft flew from Salinas to Monterey and back, taking roughly nine minutes each way. It was a piloted, coordinated flight, not the start of an autonomous urban air-taxi network. Archer itself is still working through certification, while its partners are participating in the FAA's eVTOL Integration Pilot Program.

That distinction matters. But so does the speed of progress. Electric flight is no longer a laboratory curiosity. The more interesting question for oil markets is what happens when batteries begin winning the parts of aviation they are actually suited to serve.

The Electric Aircraft Is No Longer the Science Project

The first fully electric aircraft was type-certified by EASA back in 2020. The Pipistrel Velis Electro is only a two-seat trainer, but it proved that an electric aircraft and propulsion system could pass a commercial certification process.

The technology is now moving up the scale. In 2025, EASA certified Safran's ENGINeUS 100, an electric motor platform intended to extend into applications of up to 19 seats. Heart Aerospace is developing its 30-seat ES-30, with a claimed 200-kilometre all-electric range and type certification targeted for 2031. Archer, meanwhile, is pushing the completely different eVTOL model into supervised real-world operating environments.

These aircraft will not replace a Boeing 787. They do not need to.

Road transport electrification did not begin by replacing every vehicle category at once. Buses, passenger cars and increasingly trucks electrified as battery economics and charging became suitable for each use case. Aviation is likely to be similarly uneven. Training, short cargo missions, island routes, air taxis and regional passenger services are the obvious early markets because their energy requirement is bounded and their aircraft return frequently to known infrastructure.

Where Batteries Work, the Economics Are Difficult to Ignore

The attraction is not simply that an electric aircraft has no tailpipe emissions. It is that electricity is a remarkably efficient way to produce motion. NASA is developing aviation electric machines with efficiency above 98%. Electric propulsion also offers fewer mechanically complex combustion components, lower noise and the possibility of using locally generated electricity instead of a globally traded refined oil product.

That last point looks more valuable in 2026 than it did a year ago. Middle East disruption has pushed IATA's expected average jet-fuel price for this year to $152 per barrel, around 70% above 2025, adding roughly $100 billion to the industry's fuel bill. Electricity is not immune to energy shocks, but an aircraft charged from a diversified domestic power system is not directly exposed to crude prices, refinery margins, tanker routes or a closure in the Middle East.

Related: Mexico Is Betting on Biofuel to Tackle Its Seaweed Crisis

This is where the comparison with electric cars becomes relevant. Hydrogen and synthetic fuels can technically power road vehicles. Biofuels can technically replace gasoline and diesel. But battery-electric cars increasingly won the efficiency argument because converting electricity into a fuel and then converting that fuel back into motion throws away energy and adds infrastructure.

I suspect the same will happen in aviation - but only within the range envelope where batteries work.

Jet Fuel Still Has One Enormous Advantage

The strongest objection to battery aviation is also the correct one: weight.

Jet fuel contains vastly more energy per kilogram than today's batteries, and an aircraft becomes less efficient every time extra mass must be carried into the sky. A NASA study of a notional 19-passenger electric aircraft found that roughly 600 Wh/kg at cell level would be needed to achieve a 250-nautical-mile mission with reserves - more than twice the capability assumed for then-current lithium-ion cells.

That is why sustainable aviation fuel will not follow hydrogen cars into irrelevance. Long-haul aviation needs dense liquid energy, and SAF has the huge advantage of working with aircraft and infrastructure that already exist. In 2026, however, global SAF supply is expected to reach only 2.4 million tonnes, or 0.8% of aviation fuel use. It also remains expensive.

So the likely outcome is not batteries versus SAF across all aviation. It is batteries taking the routes where electricity is technically sufficient, while SAF and eventually e-fuels fight for the much larger aircraft and longer routes where batteries remain impractical.

On those short routes, liquid fuels may eventually find themselves in the same uncomfortable position as hydrogen in passenger cars: technically possible, but economically hard to justify.

Oil Displacement Will Be Slow - Until It Isn't

The near-term oil impact should not be exaggerated. The global aircraft fleet is old enough to need renewal, but replacement is painfully slow. IATA says the aircraft order backlog has passed 18,000 units and the average fleet age has reached a record 15.2 years. Most of those aircraft on order still burn jet fuel. Certification, charging infrastructure, battery supply and airport operating procedures will slow electric adoption further.

Archer illustrates the point perfectly. The aircraft can fly. Scaling dozens or hundreds of them through constrained urban airspace, charging them quickly, turning passengers around and operating economically is a different challenge. The FAA is already building dedicated research infrastructure to study issues including vertiport operations, wake separation and downwash.

But slow adoption should not be confused with small long-term consequences.

IATA's 104 billion gallons of expected 2026 airline fuel consumption equates to roughly 6.8 million barrels per day. Electrifying just 1% of that fuel demand would displace about 68,000 barrels per day. At 10%, the arithmetic becomes roughly 0.7 million barrels per day. That is not a forecast, and today's eVTOL market will displace only a fraction of it. It simply shows why oil markets should watch regional electric aviation long before electric aircraft appear at major international gates.

Electric aviation does not have to conquer the sky to matter for oil. It only has to become the obvious choice on the routes batteries can reach. If the economics develop anything as they did on the road, that may happen faster than the existing fleet suggests.

text:
Electric aviation is moving closer to becoming a new force in regional tourism, with battery-powered aircraft expected to transform short-distance travel networks before challenging traditional long-haul aviation. While electric aircraft are not ready to replace large passenger jets, they could reshape how travellers reach islands, remote destinations, smaller cities and regional tourism hubs.

The aviation industry is entering a transition phase where different technologies will serve different travel needs. Electric aircraft are expected to dominate shorter routes where battery technology can meet operational requirements, while sustainable aviation fuel and conventional aircraft will continue supporting international long-haul journeys.

The shift could create a new tourism ecosystem built around quieter flights, lower operating costs, improved regional connectivity and access to destinations currently underserved by traditional aviation networks.

Electric Aircraft Move From Innovation To Real Aviation Operations

Electric aviation has moved beyond experimental concepts and is entering early commercial development. The sector is seeing progress across electric trainers, regional aircraft and electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft.

The first major certification milestone came when the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) certified the Pipistrel Velis Electro, becoming the world’s first fully electric aircraft to receive type certification. This demonstrated that electric propulsion systems could meet aviation safety requirements.

Further developments are now targeting larger aircraft. Electric motor technologies are being developed for regional aircraft applications, while companies such as Heart Aerospace are working on hybrid-electric aircraft designed for regional passenger operations.

At the same time, eVTOL developers are moving towards commercial air mobility services. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has been supporting advanced air mobility research and integration programmes to understand how electric aircraft can operate safely within existing aviation systems.

The transformation will not happen overnight. However, the technology is moving from research laboratories towards real-world aviation networks.

Regional Tourism Could Become The First Winner Of Electric Flights

The biggest tourism opportunity for electric aviation lies in short-distance travel.

Long-haul international aviation requires aircraft capable of carrying large passenger numbers across thousands of kilometres. Current battery technology cannot yet provide the energy density required for these operations.

However, regional tourism routes have different requirements. Many flights connect destinations located within a few hundred kilometres, making them suitable for smaller electric or hybrid-electric aircraft.

This could benefit:

Island tourism destinations

Coastal holiday regions

Rural tourism areas

Mountain destinations

Secondary cities

Remote communities

For tourism markets, electric aircraft could open new possibilities by connecting smaller airports that are currently difficult to serve economically.

A destination that lacks frequent connections because of limited passenger demand could become more accessible through smaller electric aircraft with lower operating costs.

This could encourage tourism growth in regions that are currently dependent on road transport or expensive regional flights.

Smaller Airports Could Become The New Tourism Gateways

The future of electric aviation may not begin at major international hubs such as London Heathrow, Dubai International or Singapore Changi.

Instead, smaller airports could become the first beneficiaries.

Electric aircraft require new infrastructure, including charging facilities and specialised operational systems. Regional airports with available land and flexible infrastructure may adapt faster than congested international airports.

This could create a new generation of tourism gateways.

A traveller visiting a coastal region or island destination may no longer need to fly through a major hub before taking a connecting flight. Smaller airports could offer direct regional services using quieter and more efficient aircraft.

For tourism authorities, this creates a major opportunity.

Destinations that invest early in electric aviation infrastructure could attract new visitor markets by improving accessibility and reducing transport barriers.

Airlines Could Enter A Three-Level Aviation Future

The future aviation market is unlikely to be dominated by one single technology.

Instead, airlines are expected to operate across three different segments.

Electric aircraft:

Short regional routes

Air taxis

Island connections

Training flights

Short cargo operations

Sustainable aviation fuel:

Medium-distance flights

Existing aircraft fleets

Transitional solutions for reducing emissions

Traditional jet fuel:

Long-haul international aviation

Large aircraft operations

Global connectivity

The uploaded analysis highlights that airlines are expected to consume around 104 billion gallons of fuel in 2026, showing the scale of aviation’s dependence on liquid fuels. Even a small shift towards electric aircraft could eventually influence aviation energy demand.

For tourism, this means future travel will likely combine different technologies rather than replacing one system completely.

Travellers Could Experience Quieter And More Accessible Journeys

The tourism impact of electric aviation extends beyond environmental benefits.

Electric aircraft could change the passenger experience.

Potential traveller benefits include:

Quieter flights

Electric motors produce significantly less noise compared with traditional aircraft engines. This could make flights more acceptable near residential areas and environmentally sensitive tourism locations.

More regional connections

Lower operating costs could allow airlines to introduce routes that are currently commercially challenging.

Better access to remote destinations

Small communities and tourism regions could gain improved air links.

New sustainable travel choices

Environmentally conscious travellers may increasingly prefer destinations connected through lower-emission transport options.

This aligns with the growing global demand for sustainable tourism experiences.

Battery Technology Remains The Biggest Challenge

Despite the opportunities, electric aviation faces major limitations.

The biggest challenge is battery energy density.

Aircraft require extremely high energy efficiency because every additional kilogram affects performance. Jet fuel remains far more energy dense than current battery technology.

The source analysis notes that battery limitations mean electric aviation will initially focus on short routes rather than replacing long-distance commercial flights.

Infrastructure is another challenge.

Airports will need:

High-capacity charging systems

New maintenance capabilities

Updated safety procedures

Skilled aviation workers

Aircraft certification will also determine how quickly airlines can introduce electric fleets.

Unlike road vehicles, aviation requires extremely strict safety testing, meaning commercial adoption will take time.

Electric Aviation Could Create A New Sustainable Tourism Network

The tourism industry is increasingly looking for ways to reduce emissions while maintaining global connectivity.

Electric aviation could become one part of this transformation.

Countries with island tourism economies, regional travel networks and environmentally sensitive destinations may benefit the most.

For example, short-distance tourism corridors could become ideal testing grounds for electric aircraft. A traveller could eventually fly between nearby islands, coastal cities or regional airports using aircraft designed specifically for these journeys.

This could support tourism growth while reducing dependence on large aircraft for routes where they are inefficient.

The transformation could also encourage governments and tourism authorities to rethink airport investment strategies.

Future tourism infrastructure may focus not only on large international terminals but also on smaller airports capable of supporting sustainable regional mobility.

Aviation’s Electric Future Will Begin Small But Could Grow Globally

Electric aviation will not replace jet aircraft in the immediate future. Large international aircraft will continue dominating global tourism connections for decades.

However, history shows that transport revolutions often begin in specific segments before expanding.

Electric vehicles first gained popularity in urban and passenger markets before moving into wider transport categories. Aviation could follow a similar path.

The earliest winners are likely to be regional airlines, island destinations, smaller airports and tourism markets requiring short-distance connectivity.

For travellers, the future may bring a new aviation landscape where electric aircraft provide faster access to hidden destinations and regional experiences.

For the tourism industry, electric aviation represents more than a technology shift. It could become a new connectivity model that changes how destinations compete, how airports operate and how travellers explore the world.

Electric aircraft may not replace the traditional jet age, but they could create the next major chapter in regional tourism mobility.

Overview

The global Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) logistics and supply chain market occupies a critical and rapidly expanding position at the intersection of decarbonization policy, aviation sector compliance, and advanced fuel infrastructure development. Valued at approximately USD 1.8 billion in 2024, this market encompasses the end-to-end physical and commercial ecosystem required to produce, certify, transport, blend, store, and deliver SAF to airports and airlines worldwide. As governments and international aviation bodies intensify their net-zero commitments, the logistics infrastructure underpinning SAF's commercial viability has emerged as a decisive bottleneck — and therefore a focal point for investment, strategic planning, and competitive differentiation across the energy, logistics, and aviation value chains.

Three structural forces are propelling market expansion with particular force. First, regulatory mandates across the European Union, the United States, and the United Kingdom — including the EU's ReFuelEU Aviation regulation requiring a 6% SAF blend by 2030 and the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act's blender tax credits — are converting voluntary commitments into legally enforceable offtake obligations, compelling airlines and fuel suppliers to formalize supply chains that were previously nascent or pilot-scale. Second, rapid feedstock diversification — from used cooking oil and animal fats to lignocellulosic agricultural residues, municipal solid waste, and power-to-liquid e-fuels — is generating entirely new logistics corridors, feedstock aggregation networks, and quality-assurance protocols that incumbent petroleum logistics operators must adapt to serve. Third, airline corporate sustainability commitments backed by investor pressure and CORSIA compliance requirements are driving multi-year SAF offtake agreements that, in turn, justify capital allocation toward dedicated blending terminals, pipeline modifications, and digital chain-of-custody platforms. The principal restraint on near-term growth remains a persistent and significant supply-demand imbalance: global SAF production capacity in 2024 represented less than 0.5% of total aviation fuel demand, creating severe logistical strain and elevated per-unit transport costs that compress margins across the supply chain.

Frequently asked questions

What is the size of the SAF logistics and supply chain market?

The global SAF logistics and supply chain market was valued at approximately USD 1.8 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach approximately USD 9.4 billion by 2032. In volume terms, physically delivered and logistics-handled SAF is estimated at approximately 0.6 million tonnes in 2024, reflecting the nascent but accelerating state of commercial SAF infrastructure globally.

What is the CAGR of the SAF logistics and supply chain market?

The global SAF logistics and supply chain market is forecast to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 22.8% over the 2025–2032 forecast period, driven by mandatory blending regulations, expanding feedstock pathways, and rapid scaling of dedicated transport and storage infrastructure at major aviation hubs.

What is driving growth in the SAF logistics and supply chain market?

Three principal drivers are shaping market trajectory. The EU's ReFuelEU Aviation regulation mandating a 6% SAF blend at EU airports by 2030, combined with U.S. Inflation Reduction Act blender tax credits of up to USD 1.75 per gallon, are converting aspirational targets into contractual supply chain obligations. Simultaneously, over 50 airlines have signed multi-year SAF offtake agreements exceeding 10 billion litres in aggregate, providing the revenue certainty required to finance blending terminals, feedstock aggregation hubs, and last-mile airport delivery infrastructure. Feedstock diversification — spanning used cooking oil, agricultural residues, municipal solid waste, and emerging power-to-liquid pathways — is generating entirely new international logistics corridors requiring specialized quality assurance, certification tracking, and multimodal transport solutions.

Who are the leading companies in the SAF logistics and supply chain market?

The market is shaped by a combination of SAF producers with integrated logistics capabilities and specialist fuel distribution operators. Neste Corporation of Finland is the world's largest dedicated SAF producer with over 500,000 tonnes of annual SAF capacity, supported by a global distribution network. World Energy LLC operates the first large-scale dedicated SAF production and logistics facility in the United States at Paramount, California. TotalEnergies and Shell each maintain integrated SAF production-to-wing supply chain operations across European and Asian hubs. Vopak N.V. is emerging as a critical terminal and storage infrastructure partner, while SkyNRG B.V. specializes in SAF trading, certification, and supply chain advisory services.

Which region dominates the SAF logistics and supply chain market?

Europe currently dominates the global SAF logistics and supply chain market, accounting for an estimated 44% of market revenue in 2024. This leadership reflects the region's advanced regulatory framework — including ReFuelEU Aviation and national mandates in the UK, France, and the Netherlands — the concentration of major SAF producers and blending terminal operators in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp corridor, and the high volume of transatlantic and intra-European commercial aviation routes subject to SAF compliance requirements. North America represents the second-largest region, accelerating sharply following the enactment of IRA incentives.

What segments are covered in this report?

The report segments the SAF logistics and supply chain market by feedstock-technology type — covering HEFA, Alcohol-to-Jet, Fischer-Tropsch SPK, Power-to-Liquid, and MSW-gasification pathways — and by application end-use, including commercial passenger aviation, air cargo and freight, military and defense aviation, and business and general aviation. Regional coverage spans five global regions, with granular country-level analysis for the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Singapore, and the United Arab Emirates.

This report covers a forecast period from 2025 through 2032, with 2024 serving as the base year. Historical market context is provided for the period 2019–2024 to establish pre- and post-COVID demand trajectories and the inflection point in commercial SAF supply chain development.

title: LanzaTech's Operating Expenses Fall 67% As Adjusted EBITDA Loss Improves 74%
description:
LanzaTech reduced second-quarter operating expenses by 67% year over year as an extensive cost-reduction and organizational restructuring program helped the carbon management company narrow its adjusted EBITDA loss by about 74%.
Operating expenses fell to $11.7 million from $35.1 million in Q2 2025.
Those actions reduced personnel, contractor, legal and other operating expenses as management reshaped the business around commercial project deployment.
The swing was primarily caused by a significant non-cash unrealized gain on LanzaTech’s investment in Beijing Shougang LanzaTech Technology, or SGLT.
Full-year 2026 revenue is expected to range from $50 million to $55 million, with operating expenses of $51 million to $55 million and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $22 million to $26 million.
text:
LanzaTech reduced second-quarter operating expenses by 67% year over year as an extensive cost-reduction and organizational restructuring program helped the carbon management company narrow its adjusted EBITDA loss by about 74%.

Operating expenses fell to $11.7 million from $35.1 million in Q2 2025. Adjusted EBITDA loss improved to $7.6 million from $29.7 million, representing a reduction of more than $22 million from the prior-year period.

LanzaTech attributed the improvement to transformation, cost optimization and organizational streamlining initiatives implemented during 2025. Those actions reduced personnel, contractor, legal and other operating expenses as management reshaped the business around commercial project deployment.

The company is attempting to transition from an R&D-led operating model toward one that places greater emphasis on commercial projects, technology licensing and monetization of its technology through partnerships and equity positions.

Revenue remained relatively stable despite the restructuring. Q2 revenue was $9 million compared with $9.1 million a year earlier. A $1 million decline in Joint Development Agreement revenue and a $500,000 decrease in LanzaJet sublicensing revenue were largely offset by stronger engineering and other services revenue.

Engineering and other services revenue increased to $3.3 million from $1.9 million, reflecting the initiation of new customer projects and greater engineering activity.

Reported Q2 net income reached $184.3 million compared with a $32.5 million loss in the prior-year period. The swing was primarily caused by a significant non-cash unrealized gain on LanzaTech’s investment in Beijing Shougang LanzaTech Technology, or SGLT.

The SGLT investment generated a $208.1 million non-cash unrealized gain following the joint venture’s public listing and subsequent changes in its quoted market value. SGLT completed an IPO on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in June that raised approximately $75 million and initially implied a roughly $750 million market capitalization.

By August 12, SGLT’s market capitalization had increased to approximately $1.32 billion. LanzaTech retained an approximately 8.38% interest that management estimated was worth around $110 million at that point.

LanzaTech is also progressing several commercialization initiatives. In May, the company selected North Sea Port in Ghent, Belgium, as the permanent site for its FLITE sustainable aviation fuel project. The facility is targeting annual production of 79,000 tonnes of SAF and 9,000 tonnes of renewable diesel.

Management estimates FLITE could generate approximately $115 million in annualized offtake revenue, with additional revenue opportunities possible beyond that amount.

LanzaTech is separately pursuing what it says could become the world’s first ISCC EU certification pathway for recycled carbon fuels in China. Certification would establish methodology, carbon accounting and traceability standards required to access regulated markets under the European Union’s Renewable Energy Directive and is also recognized by the U.K. Department for Transport.

Liquidity also improved during the first half. LanzaTech ended June with $48.9 million of total cash and restricted cash, compared with $17.1 million of cash, restricted cash and investments at year-end. The increase primarily reflected $50 million of gross proceeds from common-stock issuances, partially offset by operating cash usage and a $3 million investment in LanzaJet Series A preferred stock.

LanzaTech has reintroduced financial guidance following the restructuring. Full-year 2026 revenue is expected to range from $50 million to $55 million, with operating expenses of $51 million to $55 million and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $22 million to $26 million.

KEY QUOTES:

“Our Second Quarter results reflect the actions we have taken to reshape LanzaTech for the current market. We have reduced costs, renegotiated key contracts and refocused capital spend as we move from an R&D-led model toward commercial project deployment. These actions are improving our year over year operating results and creating a more disciplined platform for revenue growth and long-term profitability.”

“As we execute our near-term cost reduction and profitability improvement strategy, we continue to advance milestones that support commercialization and future value capture. Our work towards the world’s first ISCC EU certification for recycled carbon fuel is a critical step in opening mandated European fuel markets to CarbonSmart ethanol. We believe this creates new commercial optionality across multiple end markets. SAF remains a core medium-term opportunity, supported by leading alcohol-to-jet technology, while certified carbon-smart ethanol gives us near-term access to direct-use markets such as marine and road transport. That breadth is a strategic asset, giving us flexibility, resilience, and multiple paths to monetize our technology today, while certification work like ISCC EU keeps us well positioned in mandated markets as they expand. Together, these markets support our focus on converting commercial progress into revenue growth and a clearer path to sustainable profitability.”

text:
Loganair has agreed to buy five all-electric aircraft from American manufacturer BETA Technologies, a deal the Scottish carrier says will make it the first commercial airline in Europe to operate an electric fleet when the planes enter service in 2029.

The order, announced at July’s Farnborough International Airshow, covers five ALIA CX300 aircraft with an option to purchase five more. For business travellers who depend on Loganair’s regional network, the airline is promising lower operating costs and zero in-flight emissions on the short routes that link Scotland’s islands and cities with the rest of the UK.

The purchase follows a demonstration programme in the Highlands and Islands in March, when electric aircraft completed 23 flights in ten days across the airline’s network, covering more than 1,000 nautical miles.

Trials that turned a concept into an order

Chief executive Luke Farajallah said the March flying programme had answered the commercial question. “This is a truly historic moment for Loganair and for European aviation,” he said. “Our demonstration programme earlier this year proved that electric aviation is no longer a future concept, it is a viable commercial opportunity.

“The aircraft demonstrated the potential to reduce operating costs by up to 80 per cent while maintaining the reliable regional connectivity our customers and communities depend on.

“Signing this agreement is the natural next step in that journey. It reflects our confidence in the technology, our partnership with BETA, and our ambition to remain at the forefront of sustainable regional aviation. We look forward to working together as we prepare to bring these aircraft into commercial service.”

The airline said the agreement marked a “significant step towards bringing electric aviation into commercial routes across the UK” and would “ensure Loganair becomes Europe’s first commercial airline operating an electric aircraft fleet”.

How Loganair’s electric aircraft will operate

The ALIA CX300, built by Vermont-based BETA Technologies, needs no new infrastructure. It will operate from existing runways and can recharge in 20 to 40 minutes using BETA’s fast-charging systems, a turnaround short enough to suit the quick rotations that regional schedules demand. The aircraft will fly both passengers and cargo, and the agreement includes technical support and integration work so the type can slot into Loganair’s existing fleet.

Loganair said last year that a hybrid electric plane could be flying passengers from Sumburgh in Shetland to destinations such as Orkney, Aberdeen and Glasgow by 2030. The BETA order goes further, placing fully electric aircraft at the heart of the airline’s future. Travellers heading to the energy capital on those routes will find practical terminal and transfer detail in our Aberdeen airport guide.

What it means for business travellers

If the 2029 timetable holds, corporate travellers on Scotland’s lifeline and regional routes will be among the first in Europe to board scheduled all-electric services. The cost savings the airline cites matter as much as the environmental case. Thin regional routes are expensive to serve, and any reduction in operating costs improves the odds that marginal business connections survive, and could ease fare pressure over time.

Zero in-flight emissions would also be a gift for travel managers, as firms come under growing pressure to measure and cut the carbon footprint of staff travel. Electric flight offers regional aviation a nearer-term answer while the industry debates the cost and supply of sustainable aviation fuel for longer sectors.

Launching a sharp attack on the Congress government, Rao alleged that the previous BRS government had pushed Telangana into a debt burden of more than Rs 4.5 lakh crore and claimed that the Congress government had added another Rs 2 lakh crore to the State's debt within 30 months of assuming office.

He alleged that the Congress had failed to fulfil its six electoral guarantees, other poll promises and commitments relating to BC reservations.

Rao also criticised the State government over pending fee reimbursement dues, claiming that nearly Rs 12,000 crore was outstanding and alleging that the government was affecting the future of students by not implementing the New National Education Policy.

He questioned the State government for not displaying Prime Minister Narendra Modi's photograph on Smart Ration Cards.

text:
An El Niño is declared when waters in the equatorial Pacific rise 0.5 degrees Celsius above their long-term average. This naturally occurring phenomenon can shift weather systems across the globe and wreak havoc to the tune of billions - or even trillions - of dollars. But this year the results will be more extreme, combining with global warming to deliver what’s being called a “Super El Niño.” With worse droughts, bigger wildfires and larger floods, it may open a window into what climate change will look like in the future.

This means potentially catastrophic costs to commodities, supply chains and whole nations of this El Niño, which is expected to be the worst in at least 76 years. “El Niño is not just knocking on the door,” said António Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, in his address at London Climate Action Week in June. “It risks blowing the house down.”

Also read:

Heatwave and solar eclipse send Europe power prices soaring

El Niño arrives at a time when global surface air temperatures have increased by around 1.4°C since the pre-industrial era. Its effects may already be presenting themselves. Parts of Europe are experiencing record heat waves while wildfires in Spain and France have approached densely populated areas. Waterways such as the Rhine and Danube are running low, hampering transport and energy production.

In India, where June was its driest in 12 years, July brought heavy rains to Mumbai, killing at least 13 people. In the Himalayan region and across to the west coast, flash floods have killed dozens more and displaced thousands. In East Asia, Typhoon Dolphin has flooded parts of central China, with the region’s storm season shaping up to be one of the most intense on record.

Worldwide, the financial toll of this year’s event is expected to exceed $4 trillion through 2030, said Wenju Cai, a professor at Xiamen University. Such costs will far outpace extremely strong El Niño events in 2016 and 1998, he said, both “because the global economy has grown and because of the greater intensity.” In How ‘Super El Niño’ Is Turbocharging Weather Disasters, we explore what these more dramatic weather and environmental impacts may mean for the future of the planet and humanity.

Addressing the 80th Independence Day celebrations at the Police Parade Grounds here after unfurling the National Flag, receiving the Guard of Honour and inspecting the parade, Pawan Kalyan said approval had been accorded to SAF One India Espicompact for setting up the greenfield sustainable fuel manufacturing unit.

He said Kakinada was being developed as a green hydrogen production and research hub. Foundation had already been laid for a green ammonia and green hydrogen plant on 495 acres with an investment of Rs 13,000 crore, which was expected to generate employment for around 2,600 people.

Kakinada district had vast natural resources that could support industrial development and employment generation, he said, adding that the government was implementing policies aimed at promoting industrial growth.

As part of the initiative to promote entrepreneurship, the AP MSME Entrepreneur Development Policy had been formulated with the objective of creating “one industrialist-one family” by 2030, he said.

Referring to the promotion of solar power, Pawan Kalyan said rooftop solar systems had been installed in 11,933 houses in the district under the Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, creating a power generation capacity of 37,981.38 KW.

Under the SC/ST Solarisation scheme, rooftop solar plants with a capacity of two KW had been installed for 5,593 services, he said.

To ensure quality daytime power supply to the agriculture sector, solar power plants with a combined capacity of 42 MW were being established across 51 agricultural feeders under the PM-KUSUM scheme. As many as 824 free agricultural power connections had been provided up to the end of July, he said.

The government was making efforts to improve the quality of electricity supply in rural areas and ensure nine hours of uninterrupted and quality power supply to the agriculture sector, he added.

Pawan Kalyan also highlighted the progress made by the district in irrigation, housing, rural development, animal husbandry and the public distribution system.

title: Delta Air Lines' Own CEO Often Doesn't Fly In Premium Cabins: Here's Why - Simple Flying
description:
The key to Delta Air Lines' success in recent years has been the premium brand it has built.
The man behind that strategy, for the most part, is Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian.
Ed Bastian is a career operator and financier whose path to Delta Air Lines runs through both auditing and consumer goods.
He later joined Delta Air Lines in 1998 as the Vice President of Finance, before he left briefly in 2005 to serve as the CFO of Acuity Brands.
How Has Delta Air Lines Changed Under Ed Bastian's Leadership?
text:
The key to Delta Air Lines' success in recent years has been the premium brand it has built. The carrier's identity today centers around Delta One Suites, glass doors, and a wine list created by master sommeliers that includes far too many bottles to count. The man behind that strategy, for the most part, is Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian. However, he is not sitting behind those doors as you might expect. Rather, he is often in the Main Cabin or perhaps Comfort+.

Here he walks the aisles and chats with flight attendants, all while quietly trying to examine what pieces of the experience are actually more valuable to customers. It is not a marketing stunt by any stretch of the imagination, but rather a part of Ed Bastian's recurrent and extremely visible leadership philosophy, which encourages Delta leaders to listen more than they talk and make decisions anchored in what frontline employees and everyday travelers actually live through on a Tuesday afternoon flight to Atlanta.

Bastian's philosophy calls for Delta's leadership team to look beyond what boardroom slides say and to what passengers actually care about. In an era when premium cabins are the principal profit engines for airlines across the board, Bastian's choice sounds somewhat counterintuitive. Nonetheless, that is exactly the point as he observes service flows, seat ergonomics, and the pain in the boarding process that is much harder to see from seat 1A. Let's analyze why the CEO of an airline synonymous with premium travel often flies at the back of the plane.

Who Exactly Is Ed Bastian?

Ed Bastian is a career operator and financier whose path to Delta Air Lines runs through both auditing and consumer goods. A St. Bonaventure-trained accountant, Ed Bastian's career began at Price Waterhouse, where, as a young auditor, he was involved in the uncovering of a major fraud scandal at J. Water Thompson, before he moved to PepsiCo's Frito-Lay division as overseer of international finance. He later joined Delta Air Lines in 1998 as the Vice President of Finance, before he left briefly in 2005 to serve as the CFO of Acuity Brands.

He later returned to the carrier just a few months later at the request of CEO Gerald Grinstein to steer Delta through bankruptcy. In 2007, he became the airline's president and was later appointed CEO in May 2016. This mix of experiences at the carrier, which includes discipline, P&L ownership, and a front-row seat to a complex merger, alongside a turnaround under Chapter 11 bankruptcy, helps shape his style as an operator. He is known for walking the aisles and directly soliciting feedback in the Main Cabin.

This choice is consistent with his recurring advice that leadership should not be a popularity contest. He continues to cite Delta's people-first culture. Under his tenure, the airline eventually doubled down on premium products and reliability while delivering (reducing the company's overall debt burden) and expanding its partnerships with other carriers, all while his center of gravity remained operational. Bastian understands the customer, empowers employees, and keeps the carrier's overall schedule clean, all while profitability ultimately follows.

How Has Delta Air Lines Changed Under Ed Bastian's Leadership?

Since taking the helm at the carrier in 2016, Ed Bastian has steered the airline through a shift from being a large airline to a premium, reliability-led platform that features diversified earnings. From an operational perspective, Delta Air Lines rebuilt its schedule discipline and service consistency, pairing tighter operations with visible frontline engagement and faster operational recovery playbooks, all advantages that showed up during holiday travel peaks and irregular operations' resilience.

From a commercial standpoint, the airline leaned hard into overall product segmentation, with Delta One Suites and Premium Select on long-haul routes, a cleaner ladder between First, Comfort+, and the Main cabin in domestic markets. The airline also added Basic Economy to lower the fare fence for customers. Overall, network investments were matched by physical ones, including wholesale rebuilds at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) and Los Angeles International (LAX), alongside new facilities at Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

Ed Bastian pushed towards revenue diversification, pushing for a larger and more profitable SkyMiles ecosystem and scaling Delta TechOps as a third-party MRO business, alongside balance-sheet repair and overall pandemic-related deleveraging. He also kept the airline's refinery active in order to manage jet fuel exposure and advance Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) partnerships. The airline's culture remained a key part of its business model, though loyalty changes ultimately drew pushback and were modestly recalibrated.

A Deeper Look At Why Ed Bastian Flies Economy

Ed Bastian often chooses to travel economy because it keeps him close to the airline's real product and the trade-offs associated with it, according to a recent analysis from Fortune. Sitting mid-cabin allows Bastian to watch the entire passenger journey from end to end, including boarding order frictions, overhead bin availability, Wi-Fi stability, and seatback glitches, alongside galley bottlenecks and larger lavatory queues. He also believes that doing so maintains upgrade fairness, as he is not displacing a Medallion member or a paid premium customer.

This reinforces the fact that revenue and loyalty should come first. Ultimately, blending into a crowd reduces the observer effect, so he sees unscripted service and hears candid feedback from crews and travelers without the performance that follows an executive's name. It is, at the end of the day, a cultural signal that cost discipline starts at the top, especially during periods of peak passenger loads and irregular operations. This allows leaders to test the baseline before polishing fringe details within service.

From a practical standpoint, these aisle conversations surface into quick wins, including improved catering counts, cart flows, and app prompts, all of which can be fixed at last, all while chronic issues feed into larger cabin redesigns. Lastly, it helps build credibility with employees, as the CEO has felt a 31-inch pitch on a full Tuesday morning aircraft turn, debating seat intensity, boarding changes, and overall service pacing.

What Is Ed Bastian's Leadership Philosophy?

Ed Bastian's overall leadership philosophy is grounded in integrity and maintaining strong relationships with employees. He believes that leaders earn trust by showing up where work happens, listening to both customers and employees, and then making values-anchored decisions. This leads to his fairly simple leadership stack, which includes taking care of employees, who take care of customers, and thus the business ultimately takes care of itself under this model.

This eventually translates into visible, hands-on management, with regular station visits, ride-alongs, and open forums, all of which are paired with rigorous operational discipline surrounding safety, reliability, and overall costs. He prefers direct observation and data, building short feedback loops from crews and customers into its product, schedule, and technical choices. Bastian blends servant leadership with overall accountability, setting the bar high, equipping the carrier to clear it, celebrating team wins, and acknowledging his team's mistakes.

He especially values overall fairness and credibility, a key reason why he will often forgo special treatment on the road and experience the standard product himself. Culturally, he keeps purpose front and center, taking pride in service, dignity in his work, and sharing success through recognition and overall profit-sharing. The through-line is ultimately humble confidence, as he encourages leaders across the company to be present, keep promises, and let frontline truth guide overall strategy.

How Does Ed Bastian Present Delta To Investors?

Similar to his employee messaging, Ed Bastian positions Delta as a people-first business. He indicates that the carrier is a diversified premium travel platform that generates durable cash flows. He leads with operational credibility, which includes high completion factors, on-time rates, and safety protocols, all while pivoting to revenue quality, a mixed shift towards premium cabins, and continued loyalty monetization that allows the airline to outperform. This is even the case when demand is relatively weak.

Delta SkyMiles and the Amex partnership are presented as capital-light moves, both of which emerge as recurring profit engines. Delta TechOps is a third-party Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul platform that adds industrial breadth for the carrier, underscoring cost and capacity discipline on its own, all while upgauging, engaging in fleet renewal, and improving productivity. The airline follows a relatively simple capital allocation ladder, one that involves investing in product and technology, while delivering and then returning cash to shareholders.

Bastian uses cohort-style key performance indicators and clear bridge charts from operations to margin to cash, all of which create continued investor confidence. Overall risks, including fuel, labor, weather, geopolitics, and loyalty policy risks, are all addressed by mitigants and diversified partnerships. Across the board, the airline pushes forward a consumer-friendly brand, with ambition that is only constrained by the airline's balance sheet.

The Bottom Line

At the end of the day, Ed Bastian's customer-friendly attitude is emblematic of how the CEO treats both his employees and those whom he sees as guests on his flight. As the leader of an airline synonymous with service, Bastian is the best example of how Delta wants to be viewed by its passengers. The airline is the most financially successful carrier of the last decade, and for good reason.

Maintaining strong relationships with passengers has been a critical part of this pursuit, and it has allowed the airline to ensure that it can command a price premium, even in competitive domestic markets. Ultimately, Ed Bastian will leave a strong legacy at Delta Air Lines, and there is no sign that his time at the carrier is coming to an end. His ability to relate directly to customers and take their feedback into account over the years has continued to motivate his success.

text:
The Aug. 15, 2026, edition of This Week in Agribusiness covers NCGA's corn demand strategy, USDA supply and demand report market reaction, farm bill stalemate in the Senate, mandatory country of origin labeling for beef, fall soil testing best practices, and record ethanol demand.

The National Corn Growers Association is pursuing a "10-10-10" strategy targeting 10% market share in maritime fuels, sustainable aviation fuel, and bioeconomy products. Sean Arians, NCGA vice president for sustainable production, says each category could absorb up to 10 billion bushels of corn.

A USDA supply and demand report released in mid-August triggered a 20-cent single-day corn gain — the largest in roughly 18 months, according to Dan Huber of the Huber Report. Huber attributes the move partly to Russia-Ukraine disruptions shifting export demand back to the U.S.

USDA bumped corn and soybean harvested acres by over 1 million, offsetting reduced yields. Global soybean production and usage both hit a record 440 million metric tons, leaving little margin for weather disruption.

The Senate Ag Committee failed to advance the farm bill, with a SNAP cost-share provision as the central sticking point. Josh Baethge, Farm Progress policy editor, notes only 9 states fall under the 6% error-rate threshold triggering new state cost obligations beginning in October.

Mandatory country of origin labeling for beef passed the Senate Ag Committee 17–6 as part of a bipartisan amendment package. Jenna Stanton, U.S. Cattlemen's Association director of policy, called it a "huge win" after 16 years of advocacy.

Todd Spivey, Corteva technical field agronomist, recommends fall soil testing for NPK, pH and buffer capacity, using certified labs and consistent sampling methods across multiple years for reliable soil health trend data.

USDA projects a record 5.6 billion bushels of corn for ethanol in the current marketing year. Ron Lamberty, American Coalition for Ethanol chief marketing officer, says oil prices rose roughly 40% while ethanol prices rose only 10–15%, widening the blending cost advantage to as much as 20–25 cents per gallon wholesale.

Converging demand signals — from SAF and maritime fuels to record ethanol use and export growth — are reshaping the long-term outlook for corn, while near-term price direction hinges on August weather and resolution of Black Sea grain export disruptions.

text:
Hong Kong: Cathay Pacific has discontinued passenger services to 16 long-haul destinations from its Hong Kong hub over the past two decades, with several routes dropped during the Covid-19 pandemic, according to reports.

The destinations were identified by comparing Cathay Pacific’s passenger network between January 2006 and July 2026 with services scheduled through May 2027. The review covers only long-haul routes from Hong Kong International Airport.

The most recent route to disappear is Cairns in Australia. Cathay Pacific resumed seasonal flights to Cairns in December 2024 but has no services to the destination scheduled for 2026 or 2027.

Other discontinued destinations include Jeddah, Abu Dhabi, Karachi, Moscow, Doha, Copenhagen, Düsseldorf, Dublin, Bahrain, Cape Town, Malé, London Gatwick, Newark, Washington Dulles and Tel Aviv.

Nearly 40 percent of the cuts took place in 2020 as the pandemic prompted airlines to reassess networks and fleet deployment.

Cathay Pacific also ended services to Washington Dulles in 2020 after operating the route for less than two years. The service ran four times weekly between September 2018 and February 2020, using Airbus A350 aircraft.

Despite the cuts, the destinations remain accessible to Cathay passengers through its alliance and codeshare partners.
